subject: Food Science
title: Salmonella
description: A quick, practical guide to Salmonella.

hook.text: Salmonella infects 1.35 million Americans every year. Raw eggs and undercooked chicken are the usual suspects.

buildup.text: Salmonella lives in animal intestines and contaminates meat, eggs, and produce through fecal contact during processing.

discovery.text: It takes as few as 10–100 Salmonella cells to cause infection—an invisibly small dose on a contaminated surface.

twist.text: Washing raw chicken spreads Salmonella via water splash up to 3 feet around the sink. The USDA says: don't wash chicken.

climax.text: Cooking to 74°C kills Salmonella reliably. A meat thermometer is the only way to know you've reached safety.

punchline.text: Don't wash your chicken. Do cook it thoroughly. That's the Salmonella rule.

quiz.question: Why does the USDA say not to wash raw chicken?
options: Water spreads Salmonella up to 3 feet around the sink
